title: The Dragonfly in Two Summers
creature: A dragonfly who is in this summer and one other
summary: Elin sees the pond twice at once, and there is a boy on the far bank who is not there.

chapters.title: The Pond at Cwm Bach
chapters.text: The pond is not much and Elin would like that clear, because people hear about it and imagine somewhere. It is about forty metres across and it is in a dip in a field below the farm, and it has reeds along the north side and a willow that came down in 2015 and has gone on growing lying down, and it has a wooden thing at one end that was a jetty in about 1970 and is now four posts. Her family have farmed above it since 1911. Elin has swum in it. Her father learned to swim in it. There are newts in it and in April there is frogspawn and in a hot July it smells. It is on the farm's land and nobody outside the family has been down there in years. There is no path to it and no sign and no reason for anybody to go, and the gate at the top of the field has been tied with the same orange baler twine since about 2012. The dragonfly is a golden-ringed and it is the largest species in Britain, which is not saying an enormous amount — about eight centimetres — and it is black with yellow bands and green eyes that meet in the middle. There is one on that pond every summer. Not the same one. Elin is entirely clear about this and gets slightly short with people who want it to be the same one: a golden-ringed dragonfly lives as an adult for a few weeks and spends the previous two to five years as a larva in the mud, and there is no version of the biology in which an insect on that pond in 1994 is an insect on that pond in 2024. What is the same is the reed. Elin has thought about whether that is even remarkable and has decided it probably is not. A dragonfly perch is a position, not a plant: a stem that stands clear at a particular height with a particular view of the water and the sun behind it in the afternoon. If the geometry of a pond stays the same, the best perch stays the same, and a reed clump on a bank stays where it is for decades. That is almost certainly the whole of it. It lands on the same reed. Third from the left of the clump at the north end, about sixty centimetres up, facing the water. Elin has counted from the left every time and has been careful to count from the same end, which sounds obvious and which she got wrong twice before she made herself write down which end the willow was at. Elin has photographs from four different summers and her father has one from about 1996 that his mother took, and it is the same reed clump and it is very nearly the same position within it, and Elin has no explanation for this at all and does not think it is the interesting part.

chapters.title: The Slip
chapters.text: The first time happened in the July she was eleven and it lasted about four seconds. She was lying on the bank on her front, about three metres from the reeds, watching it. It had been there for perhaps a minute doing the thing they do, which is nothing whatsoever with the body while the head goes round. Then it took off, and came back, and landed in the same place. It is worth saying what that looks like at three metres, because most people have only seen dragonflies going past. It does not flutter and it does not settle. It goes from stationary to about eight metres away in something under a second, in a straight line, and then it is stationary again in mid-air over the water — properly stationary, not hovering with effort — and then it is back on the reed, and the whole excursion has taken perhaps three seconds and there has been no part of it in which the animal looked like it was making an effort. And the pond changed. Not dramatically and not all at once and not, at first, in any way she could name. Something about the light. Something about the noise, which went slightly down. Then she saw the willow. The willow was standing up. It came down in the January of 2015 in a gale and Elin had been in the kitchen when it went and had heard it, and she had walked past its trunk lying in the water every summer of her conscious life. And there it was, upright, on the far bank, in leaf, a different shape entirely. She looked at the rest of it and the jetty had planks on it. And there was a boy on the far bank. He was sitting on the end of the jetty with his feet not in the water and he was doing nothing. He had his elbows on his knees. He was perhaps eleven or twelve and he was wearing a red T-shirt and he was looking at the reeds at the north end, which is to say approximately at her, and he did not react in any way at all. Then the dragonfly moved, and the willow was lying down, and the jetty was four posts, and the bank was empty. Nothing came with it. No sound, no cold, no smell, none of the things people ask about. The transition in both directions was instantaneous and she did not feel it happen either time; there was a pond, and then there was a different pond, and then there was the pond. Elin lay on the grass for a considerable time. She was eleven. What she did about it, over the following week, was to construct four explanations, of which the strongest was that she had fallen asleep in the sun, and she was reasonably satisfied with that until it happened again at thirteen while she was standing up.

chapters.title: Which Summer
chapters.text: She worked out the year over about two years, and she did it the boring way, which was photographs. There are perhaps two thousand photographs of that farm in three boxes and a biscuit tin, and Elin went through all of them twice between the ages of eleven and thirteen, on the floor of the back bedroom, and told her mother she was doing a project. The willow standing up gives you before January 2015. The jetty with planks on it is harder; her father reckoned the planks came off in the late nineties and her grandmother said 1997 and there is a photograph from a christening in 1999 in which they are already gone. So: before 1999. And then she had the T-shirt, which is not much of a clue, and the boy, who was somebody's child on their own land in a valley of four farms. She had ruled her uncle out on height and there were no other boys of that age in the valley in the nineties, which left one candidate and which she had known perfectly well from about the fourth second and had spent two years not looking at directly. She got it in the end from a box in the back bedroom. It is a photograph from the summer of 1994 of her father, aged eleven, on the end of that jetty, with his elbows on his knees, in a red T-shirt. It is not the same moment. She has been very careful about this and has looked at that photograph perhaps a thousand times: in the picture he is looking at the camera and slightly annoyed, and the boy she saw was looking at the reeds and was not annoyed at all. It is the same afternoon, or the same fortnight, or the same summer. It is not the same second. Which matters, because the obvious explanation is that she saw the photograph as a small child, forgot it, and reassembled it on a hot afternoon at eleven. Elin thinks that is probably what happened. She has said so out loud to the two people she has told. It accounts for the boy and the T-shirt and the jetty and even the willow, because the willow is standing up in about four hundred other photographs in those boxes. What it does not account for is the second one, at thirteen, standing up, in which there was a bicycle on the grass — and there is no photograph of a bicycle by that jetty in any of the three boxes or the tin, and she has looked, and her father says he had a bicycle then and used to leave it exactly there. Elin was thirteen when she worked it out and she did not tell anybody for nine years.

chapters.title: What She Told Him
chapters.text: It has happened to her four times. Eleven, thirteen, sixteen, and twenty-two. Always at that pond, always with the dragonfly on that reed, always between three and six seconds, always the same summer on the other side. She has been down to that pond, on a conservative estimate, four hundred times. She has lain on that bank in July with a dragonfly on that reed perhaps sixty times. Four. That is the rate, and she puts it in whenever she tells this, because a story about a thing that happens is a completely different story from a story about a thing that has happened four times in eighteen years to one person with nobody else there. She has never seen the boy again. Three of the four times there was nobody on the far bank at all; once there was a bicycle lying on the grass by the jetty. She has no mechanism and she is not going to offer one. What she has is four occasions, two of which happened after she was old enough to be sceptical about the first two, and a photograph that she found afterwards and not before, which she thinks is the only part of the account that would interest anybody who does this properly. She told her father in the November she was twenty-two, at the kitchen table, badly, over about twenty minutes. He listened all the way through without interrupting, which is not like him. Then he said: "Red T-shirt." "Yes." "I had that until I was about thirteen. My mother hated it." He turned his cup round. "What was I doing?" "Nothing. Sitting on the jetty with your elbows on your knees looking at the reeds." And her father sat there for a while and then said the thing that Elin was not remotely prepared for, which was: "That'll be the summer my father was ill." He said that he had spent most of that July down at that pond because there was nothing to do at the house and because there were people in it all the time, and that he had sat on that jetty for hours, and that he could not now remember one single thing he had thought about in the whole of that month. He said he had been fine. He said he was not saying it had been bad. He said that when he thought about that summer at all what he got was the pond and the heat and the smell of it and nothing else, and that he had never told anybody that and had not known he was going to tell her. Her grandfather recovered, as it happens, and lived until 2011, and Elin knew him and he taught her to reverse a trailer. That is the part that nearly everybody gets wrong when she tells it. They want the summer to have been the last one. It was not. It was an ordinary frightening summer in the middle of a life that turned out fine, and the thing her father could not remember a single thought from was eleven weeks of being a boy at a pond while adults he loved were doing something difficult upstairs. Elin is twenty-nine. She goes down to the pond in July, most years, and lies on the bank on her front about three metres from the reeds, and waits for a dragonfly that is not the same dragonfly to land on the third reed from the left. She has never once thought of anything she would say.
